inline.s: [That land does not turn away; it is drawn by its own nature] The Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss does not reject any sentient being (that land does not turn away), but the reason sentient beings cannot be reborn there is that at death they cannot maintain right mindfulness and the intermediate states (yīnjìng) appear, and so they follow the force of karma to be reborn in the six destinies, utterly unable to be their own masters (drawn by their own nature).

“The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings have faith and vows complete, and sincerely sense the Buddha, the Buddha responds, as when the water is clear the moon appears. If the mind is not pure and sincere, accords with greed, anger, and delusion, and turns away from the Buddha, it is like water that is muddy and moving; though the moon does not fail to shine upon it, its reflection cannot be clearly manifested.”

The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings have complete faith and vows and sincerely sense the Buddha, the Buddha responds, as when the water is clear and still the moon appears (a metaphor: the pure mind of right mindfulness senses Amitabha Buddha's coming to receive and guide). If the mind is not pure, not sincere, accords with greed, anger, and delusion, and turns away from the Buddha, it is like muddied, agitated water; though the Buddha-moon does not fail to shine upon it, its reflection cannot be clearly manifested (a metaphor: an agitated, muddy, deluded mind cannot sense Amitabha Buddha's coming to receive and guide).

“The moon is but a form-dharma of the world, and yet it has such wonder. How much more so Amitabha Buddha, who has utterly purified afflictions and delusions, is complete in merit and wisdom, whose mind encompasses the great emptiness, whose measure extends throughout the dharma-realm? Therefore the Avatamsaka Sutra says: ‘The Buddha's body fills the dharma-realm, manifesting everywhere before all sentient beings; responding to conditions it never fails to reach them, while ever dwelling on this bodhi-seat.’ Hence we know that the response pervades the dharma-realm, and the resonance pervades the dharma-realm. The Buddha has truly never stirred his mind or thought, nor has any mark of coming or going, and yet he can cause sentient beings whose conditions are ripe to see him come here to receive and guide them to the West.”

The moon is but a form-dharma of the world and yet has such wonder. How much more so Amitabha Buddha, who has utterly purified afflictions and delusions, is complete in merit and wisdom, whose mind encompasses the great emptiness and whose measure extends throughout the dharma-realm? Therefore the Avatamsaka Sutra says: “The Buddha's body fills the dharma-realm, manifesting everywhere before all sentient beings; responding to conditions it never fails to reach them, while ever dwelling on this bodhi-seat.” Hence we know: sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm respond (sense), and Amitabha Buddha throughout the dharma-realm resonates. Amitabha Buddha has truly never stirred his mind or thought, never had any mark of coming or going, and yet he can cause sentient beings whose conditions are ripe to see him come here to receive and guide them to the West.
The Sutra of Praising the Merit of the Buddhas says:
“When life is about to end, if one has single-minded faith and joy, with a thought that does not forget or abandon, Amitabha Buddha, leading
(bringing)
the assembly of monks
(Śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas)
, stands before that person; the māras can never destroy this
(this person's)
mind of right awakening.”
Master Xing'an (the eleventh Patriarch of the Pure Land school) says:

“Suppose one is upside-down in a single thought at death — not only will one not be born in the nine grades, one can scarcely avoid the three lower paths; though the Buddha is greatly compassionate, he cannot save me. Alas! Alas!”
(from the Debate on Demonic Possession in Reciting the Buddha's Name)
Master Yinguang says:
“At the time of death, by one's own pure mind, one senses the Buddha's receiving and guidance to be reborn in the West.”
(from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, Reply to the Layman Gu Zongkuang)
Master Yinguang, speaking of the principle of Amitabha Buddha's receiving and guiding sentient beings who recite the Buddha's name at the time of death, says:

“The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings have faith and vows complete, and sincerely sense the Buddha, the Buddha responds, as when the water is clear the moon appears. If the mind is not pure and sincere, accords with greed, anger, and delusion, and turns away from the Buddha, it is like water that is muddy and moving; though the moon does not fail to shine upon it, its reflection cannot be clearly manifested.”
(from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, Preface to the Guide to Pure Karma for Beginners)

Therefore Master Yinguang, in his Three Essentials at the Time of Death, instructs: “Now I set forth the three essentials as the basis for helping the dying attain rebirth. Though the words are plain and vulgar, the meaning is from the Buddha's scriptures; when encountering this occasion, put them all into practice. The three essentials are: first, skillfully guide and comfort, to give rise to right faith; second, all present should take turns reciting the Buddha's name to aid the pure mindfulness; third, strictly refrain from moving the body and from weeping, to prevent mishaps.” These three essentials are all to cause the dying to give rise to right mindfulness, to gather it, to maintain it, and to sense the Buddha's coming to welcome.

The questioner says: The view that “right mindfulness at death and the Buddha's coming to welcome” is correct — rather, “the Buddha's coming to welcome, and one abides in right mindfulness,” is right.

Master Hōnen says: “Moreover, one who truly has the resolve for rebirth, who believes in Amitabha's primal vow and recites the Buddha's name — such a person is not upside-down at death. The reason is that the Buddha's coming to welcome is precisely for the sake of the practitioner's right mindfulness at death. Those who do not understand this all think that it is their own right mindfulness at death and [that only when] reciting does the Buddha come to welcome; this view repudiates the primal vow and also does not know the scriptures. The Sutra of Praising the Pure Land says: ‘Compassion and aid, causing the mind not to be confused.’

“When one constantly recites [the Buddha's name] in daily life, the Buddha will surely come to welcome; once one sees the Buddha appear, one abides in right mindfulness. Therefore do not think that reciting is in vain, and [do not think] that merely praying for right mindfulness at death is correct — such a view is very mistaken. Hence one who believes in Amitabha's primal vow must not harbor doubt about the mind at death. Even for one who only recites at the time of death, Amitabha also made the vow to come and welcome. One who attains rebirth by reciting at death — originally he had no vow for rebirth, but was an evil being given over to sin; at the moment of death, encountering a good companion's urging, he recites and is reborn — the Contemplation Sutra also speaks of this. If one is a person of constant recitation, one need not forcefully judge the marks at death. Because the Buddha's coming to welcome is certain, the right mindfulness at death is likewise certain; this principle should be borne in mind.””
Answer: In the Sutra of Praising the Pure Land (
the Sutra of Praising the Buddha's Reception of the Pure Land
), the passage “compassion and aid, causing the mind not to be confused” runs:

“If there are pure-hearted good men or good women who, having heard the immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable name of merit of Amitāyus Buddha and the merit and adornment of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, reflect upon it after hearing — for one day and night, or two or three, or four or five, or six or seven,
with thought not confused (single-mindedness)
. If
(this)
good man or good woman, at the moment of death, [with] Amitāyus Buddha together with his immeasurable Śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas, surrounding front and back,
comes and stands before him
, with compassion and aid,
causing the mind not to be confused

. Once life has been laid down, following the Buddha's assembly, he is born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus.” The World-Honored One here clearly instructs: the good man or good woman who, in reciting the Buddha's name, keeps the thought not confused
(single-mindedness)

, “at the moment of death, [with] Amitāyus Buddha together with his immeasurable Śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas, surrounding front and back, comes and stands before him, with compassion and aid, causing the mind not to be confused.”
Therefore the premise of the Buddha's
“coming to stand before him, with compassion and aid, causing the mind not to be confused”
is that this dying person has already attained thought-not-confused (single-mindedness)
Therefore the World-Honored One in this sutra says: reciting the Buddha's name to reach thought-not-confused (single-mindedness), the Buddha
will surely
come to welcome. Yet Master Hōnen twisted the text into: “When one constantly recites in daily life, the Buddha
will surely

come to welcome.” And then he rebukes: “Those who do not understand this all think it is their own right mindfulness at death when reciting that the Buddha comes to welcome; this view repudiates the primal vow and also does not know the scriptures.” May I ask: who, in the end, is the one who does not know the scriptures?
Q: Since “this good man or good woman” has already attained thought not confused, why does it say that after Amitabha Buddha comes, “with compassion and aid, causing the mind not to be confused”?

Answer: Thought not confused is what senses the Buddha's coming to welcome, but thought not confused is a shallower level of practice, often not enough to keep the mind from confusion at the time when the four great elements dissolve and suffering presses and demons appear, and that is why Amitabha Buddha “with compassion and aid causes the mind not to be confused.” The Sutra of Praising the Merit of the Buddhas says:
“When life is about to end, with single-minded faith and joy, with a thought that does not forget or abandon
this is right mindfulness at death
, Amitabha Buddha, leading
(bringing)
the assembly of monks
(Śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas)
, stands before that person; the māras can never destroy this
(this good man or good woman's)
mind of right awakening.”

Moreover, in this sutra (the Sutra of Praising the Pure Land), after speaking of thought not confused (single-mindedness), the World-Honored One emphasizes again and again, over and over, the requirement to
practice as taught
. The “practice as taught” spoken of here means that faith, vows, and the holding of the Name must attain thought not confused (single-mindedness). And he clearly tells us:
only by practicing as taught

is one received and embraced by the Buddhas of the ten directions, and will surely be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and will never withdraw, quickly realizing the fruit of Buddhahood — his concern overflowing in the words. How could it be that merely having faith suffices for “at the moment of death, [with] Amitāyus Buddha together with his immeasurable Śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas, surrounding front and back, comes and stands before him, with compassion and aid, causing the mind not to be confused”?
The World-Honored One instructs:

“If there are pure-hearted good men or good women, who have heard such inconceivable merit of the Name of Amitāyus Buddha and the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they should all believe, receive, and make the vow,
practice as taught
, and be born in that Buddha-land.”

“Those who practice as taught will all, for certain, be irrevocable from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and will all, for certain, be born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus Buddha. Therefore, Śāriputra, all you sentient beings should believe, accept, and comprehend the words of me and the Buddhas of the ten directions, and diligently progress,
practicing as taught
, without giving rise to doubt.”
Those who practice as taught

, all for certain, from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi are irrevocable; all for certain are born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus Buddha. Therefore, Śāriputra, if there are pure-hearted good men or good women, they should all, with deep mind, believe and understand the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus, make the vow for rebirth,
and not be given to negligence

“In this defiled world of endurance, in the time of the five turbidities, if there are pure-hearted good men or good women, who, having heard this most-difficult-to-believe Dharma of all the world, can give rise to faith and understanding, and receive, uphold, expound, and
practice as taught

, know that such a person is most rare, having planted good roots in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas. At the end of life, such a person will surely be born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and enjoy the various meritorious adornments of the pure Buddha-land and the Mahāyāna bliss of the Dharma.”

As for the case in the Contemplation Sutra of “evil beings given over to past sins who, at the time of death, first encounter a good companion's urging and recite [the Buddha's name]” and so attain rebirth, Master Yinguang says:

“The Contemplation Sutra [speaks of] the five rebellious acts and the ten evil deeds; when about to die, the marks of hell appear. There is a good companion (original note: this does not distinguish monk or lay, man or woman; whoever can teach that person to recite [the Buddha's name] is called a good companion) who teaches him to recite the Buddha's name — perhaps only ten recitations, perhaps not even ten — and he directly dies, and still, relying on the Buddha's compassionate power, is reborn while carrying his karma. These ten recitations, compared with ordinary ten recitations, have a fierce and urgent force utterly different as heaven from the abyss, and that is why he is reborn. Driven by the extreme suffering of hell, the instant he hears the Buddha's name, he recites it with his entire being.
Apart from this recitation, there is absolutely no other thought. Though he has not personally realized single-mindedness, his mind is nonetheless without any different thought.”
(from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, Reply to the Layman Chen Xinru.) Moreover, for such a person so able to be reborn, Master Ouyi adds:
“This is one in ten thousand; how could one depend on luck!”
(from the Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sutra)

The questioner says: Master Taixu, in his Principle of Rebirth through Reciting the Buddha's Name, says: “Relying on the power of the good Dharma is faith; resolving to be reborn is the power of vows. If faith and vows are truly determined and firm, then whether the practice is shallow or deep, one can be reborn; it is only that with deeper practice the grade is higher.” So, as long as faith and vows are truly determined and firm, whether the practice is shallow or deep, one can be reborn.

Answer: Among faith, vows, and practice, the purpose of practice is to make faith and vows truly determined and firm, so that at the moment of death one can attain clear right mindfulness, and thereby ensure rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Can the absence of practice, or shallow practice, achieve this? The Buddha in the scriptures repeatedly warns to “practice as taught,” and the patriarchs repeatedly say “by practice fulfill vows; by practice authenticate faith.” Why always tear practice apart from faith and vows, and speak of practice as if it were of no consequence? (Think deeply!) As if, apart from diligent, strenuous, vigorous recitation, one could make faith and vows truly determined and firm and have clear right mindfulness at death. Does this accord with the Buddha's words, the patriarchs' words, and the actual situation? In truth, I need not wait until death: even now you may test it. Can you, in joy or in anger, maintain clear right mindfulness? By this you can discern whether your faith and vows are truly determined and firm, and where you will go at the time of death.

Q: Master Taixu, in his Principle of Rebirth through Reciting the Buddha's Name, says: “The power of vows — the power of the vow-force — is inconceivable: it is the extremely sincere will-power produced by concentrating the mind's force. As when a person who recites the Buddha's name makes the vow for rebirth: at that moment making the vow, concentrating the mind's force on the vow for rebirth, over time maturing it, achieving the vow-force formed by practice — from the function accomplished by this vow-force, one can discover a result beyond the ordinary, produced by a conceivable causal force.” Does not “concentrating the mind's force on the vow for rebirth and, over time, maturing it” — with such firm faith and vows — surely entail rebirth?

Answer: “Concentrating the mind's force on the vow for rebirth and, over time, maturing it” — this IS practice, and very vigorous practice; and the conclusion in the same passage, “whether the practice is shallow or deep,” is self-contradictory with this. May I ask: can a shallow practice achieve “maturing over time”? You can verify this yourself.

The questioner says: Master Taixu, in his Principle of Rebirth through Reciting the Buddha's Name, says: “Even if one has not achieved good roots, so long as one believes in the power of the good Dharma, together with the earnest power of vows in one's own mind, one thereby achieves good roots, and can interpenetrate with the power of Amitabha Buddha's vows; what the power of Amitabha Buddha's vows accomplishes becomes what one's own vow-power accomplishes, and one can claim a share in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Here is a very ordinary example: suppose a rich man makes a will leaving all his property to aid the disabled throughout the whole world. If at that moment there is a person who is already disabled, then this person has a share in the rich man's bequeathed property. One who vows for rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss thereby has a share in the Land — it is just the same.”

Answer: In the chapter on the Perfect Penetration through Reciting the Buddha's Name by Mahasthamaprapta, he, too, offers a simile. Suppose there are two men, A and B. A directs his whole mind to thinking of B, while B does not think of A at all. Such two people — even if they meet, it is as if they had not met; perhaps they see each other, and it is as if they had not seen. If both direct their whole minds to thinking of each other, then their thoughts of longing grow deeper and deeper, engraved into their very bones, so that from life to life, in life after life, for generation after generation, they are inseparable as shadow from form, of one feeling and one body, never apart or abandoned. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, compassionately loving and thinking of sentient beings, are like a mother thinking of her child. If the child runs away, though the mother thinks of him, what use is such constant longing to the child? If the child thinks of his mother as the mother thinks of him, then mother and child, from life to life, are neither adverse nor far apart. If the minds of sentient beings recollect the Buddha and recite the Buddha's name until the practice matures into one, then in the present or the future they will surely see the Buddha, not far from Buddhahood; without relying on any other means, the mind will open of itself. (The original text:

“It is like a person — one wholly recollecting, the other wholly forgetting; such two people, if they meet it is as if they had not met, or if they see, it is as if they had not seen. If the two recollect each other, their recollections grow deep, until from life to life they are like shadow and form, never diverging. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, compassionately thinking of sentient beings, are like a mother thinking of her child; if the child runs away, though the mother thinks of him, what use is it? If the child thinks of his mother as the mother thinks of him, then mother and child, from life to life, are neither adverse nor far apart. If the minds of sentient beings recollect the Buddha and recite the Buddha's name, in the present or the future they will surely see the Buddha, not far from Buddhahood; without relying on means, the mind will open of itself.”
) Which of the two similes do you think is appropriate?
